232.title: Four rooms to live in
232.hook: kindness, compassion, gladness for others, equanimity: the "divine abodes" (DN 13)
232.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions practice the four brahmaviharas, often by sending each quality out in all directions; Theravada teachers use them as meditation subjects, and Mahayana teachers speak of them as the heart of the bodhisattva's path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, appamada, and your line: you actually read it. Today, camp five begins: the depths.

Where does your mind spend most of the day? Not your body, your mind. For a lot of people, it's a few familiar rooms. The worry room. The irritation room, with the window that looks out on other people's mistakes. The comparison room, lined with other people's photos. Nobody chooses to go in. A mind just finds itself there, again and again, out of habit. The Buddha described four other rooms, and taught a way to move into them.
screen: `WHERE DOES YOUR MIND LIVE?` → `WORRY, IRRITATION, COMPARISON.` → `FOUR OTHER ROOMS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is brahmavihara. Brahma means divine, sublime, the highest. Vihara means a dwelling, a place you live; it's also the word for a monastery. So brahmavihara is a divine abode, a sublime place to live. There are four. Metta, kindness: wishing others well. Karuna, compassion: being moved by another's pain. Mudita, gladness at someone else's good fortune. And upekkha, equanimity: a balance that doesn't abandon anyone. They're also called the four immeasurables, because they can grow without limit. In the discourse on the three knowledges, two young brahmins come to the Buddha arguing about which teacher knows the way to union with Brahma, the god they worshiped. The Buddha doesn't mock their question. He answers in their own language. Someone who wants to live with Brahma, he says, should let a mind of kindness fill one direction, then the second, the third and the fourth, then above, below and all around, the whole world, boundless and free of hatred. Then compassion the same way, then gladness, then equanimity. Buddhists read this in different ways. Theravada teachers stress it as a meditation that calms the mind and supports insight. Mahayana teachers see the four as the heart of the bodhisattva, who works for the good of all beings. You met metta in camp three. The next two weeks walk through each room, along with what the old manuals call each room's enemies: a far enemy that's its opposite, and a near enemy that looks just like it.
screen: `BRAHMA — DIVINE; VIHARA — A DWELLING.` · `KINDNESS, COMPASSION, GLADNESS, BALANCE.` · `TWO YOUNG BRAHMINS ASK THE WAY.` · `EACH ROOM HAS TWO ENEMIES.` · then, large: `FOUR ROOMS TO LIVE IN.`

segments.voice: Stand in each doorway for a few breaths. Metta: let a warm wish for someone arise; karuna: remember someone who's struggling, and let your heart soften; mudita: think of someone who's doing well, and be glad; upekkha: let everything be as it is, for this moment. Then rest in whichever room felt most like home.
Brahmavihara. A divine abode: kindness, compassion, gladness for others and equanimity, the four rooms to live in.
Your line: boundless and free of hatred. Four rooms, each able to grow without limit. That's day two hundred thirty-two.

a rule for how monks share their meals

233.title: Metta, revisited
233.hook: kindness wishes well; its near enemy is clinging affection (Visuddhimagga 9)
233.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions teach the near and far enemies from the Visuddhimagga, so students can tell real kindness from its look-alikes; metta practice often begins with oneself or a benefactor rather than a romantic partner.

segments.voice: Yesterday: brahmavihara, the four rooms of kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity. Your line: boundless and free of hatred. Today, the first room, again.

Some love feels like a gift, and some feels like a grip. The friend who's glad when good things happen to you, even when it means you move away. And the one whose affection comes with strings: text me back, need me, don't change. Both call it love. Both might even feel warm from the inside. But one leaves you free and the other doesn't. A Buddhist manual written fifteen hundred years ago drew exactly this line.
screen: `A GIFT, OR A GRIP.` → `LOVE WITH STRINGS.` → `ONE LEAVES YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: You met metta in camp three: kindness, loving-kindness, from mitta, a friend. The phrases, the benefactor, the difficult person, the six directions. Now i want to go deeper, with the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, a great manual of meditation written in Sri Lanka by the monk Buddhaghosa in the fifth century. Its ninth chapter maps each of the four rooms. Metta's mark, it says, is promoting the welfare of others. Its job is to prefer their welfare. It shows up as the melting away of ill will. Then the surprise: every room has two enemies. The far enemy is the obvious opposite, easy to spot. The near enemy is sneakier: it looks like the real thing, feels like it, and quietly takes its place. For metta, the near enemy is greed, clinging affection, attachment that wants something back. It's near, the manual explains, because both kindness and clinging notice what's good in a person. One says, may you be well. The other says, may you be mine. So metta succeeds when it makes ill will fade, and fails when it turns into sticky, selfish affection. That's why the manual suggests starting not with a romantic partner, where the line blurs easily, but with yourself, and then a benefactor, someone who has helped you, like a teacher. None of this means affection is wrong. Families and friendships run on it. The point is to know the difference from the inside: kindness wishes well, and lets go.
screen: `METTA — FROM MITTA, A FRIEND.` · `THE MAP OF THE VISUDDHIMAGGA.` · `NEAR ENEMY: CLINGING AFFECTION.` · `MAY YOU BE WELL, NOT MAY YOU BE MINE.` · then, large: `KINDNESS, NOT CLINGING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love and offer the old wish silently: may you be well, may you be happy. Then look gently underneath it for a string, a wanting them to stay, to need you, to turn out a certain way, and if you find one, just see it, without scolding yourself. Then wish again with the string cut: may you be well, however your life turns out.
Metta. Kindness that wishes others well; its near enemy is clinging affection, which looks warm but wants something back.
Your line: kindness, not clinging. The first room, with its look-alike at the door. See you tomorrow.

234.title: Metta's far enemy
234.hook: ill will is metta's opposite; kindness dissolves it slowly
234.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on the Visuddhimagga's methods for softening resentment, such as recalling a person's good qualities or giving a gift, and practitioners send metta to difficult people in small, gradual steps.

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta, revisited, and its near enemy, clinging affection. Your line: kindness, not clinging. Today, the enemy that looks nothing like it.

The coworker who chews loudly. The neighbor who parks across your driveway. The relative who always makes that one comment at dinner. Ill will rarely starts big. It starts as an irritation, and then it gets fed: replayed in the shower, told to a friend, rehearsed in imaginary arguments where you always win. After a while, just seeing the person's name can tighten a jaw.
screen: `THE LOUD CHEWER, THE DRIVEWAY.` → `IRRITATION, FED AND REPLAYED.` → `THE JAW TIGHTENS.`

segments.voice: The Visuddhimagga names metta's far enemy plainly: ill will, the Pali vyapada, the wish for someone to suffer. It's called far because it's the opposite of kindness, and easy to recognize. The danger isn't mistaking it. The danger is that it's comfortable, and it grows. So the manual gives a whole toolkit for softening it, one method after another, for when the first doesn't work. One tool: look at what anger does to the one who holds it. The manual compares it to picking up a burning coal to throw at someone: your own hand gets burned first. Another: look for one good quality in the person, even a small one. If their actions are rough, maybe their speech is kind; if not that, maybe their heart has something good in it. The manual compares this to a traveler, hot and thirsty, who finds a pond covered in moss, sweeps the moss aside with his hands, and drinks. Another: everyone is the owner of their own actions; your anger won't fix theirs. One is disarmingly simple: give the person a gift. The manual says a gift can soften a long-held grudge in a moment. And one of the strangest: take the person apart, in your mind, into hair, skin, bones, warmth and breath, and ask, which part am I angry at? It's hard to stay angry at an elbow. None of this is quick. Kindness dissolves ill will slowly, the way water wears down stone. You met the root of this in the Dhammapada's fifth verse: hatred never ends by hatred. Here is the practical how.
screen: `VYAPADA — ILL WILL.` · `THE BURNING COAL.` · `SWEEP THE MOSS AND DRINK.` · `A GIFT, AND WHICH PART AM I ANGRY AT?` · then, large: `ILL WILL SOFTENS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small irritation, one person who annoys you a little, and notice where it lives in your body. Then sweep the moss aside and find one good quality in them, however small: they love their dog, they're kind to the cashier, they work hard. If you can, offer them one breath of the old wish, may you be well, and notice any softening.
Byāpāda. Ill will, the plain opposite of kindness: the manual's tools soften it slowly, one method at a time.
Your line: ill will softens. A whole toolkit, for when the first tool doesn't work. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

235.title: Karuna
235.hook: compassion: the heart that trembles at another's pain
235.howItsDone: Buddhists practice karuna both as a meditation, extending the wish that beings be free of suffering, and in action; across traditions it is one of the four divine abodes, and in Mahayana traditions it stands at the heart of the bodhisattva ideal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: byāpāda, ill will, and the manual's toolkit for softening it. Your line: ill will softens. Today, the second room.

You're scrolling, and a photo stops you. A child in a flood, a man sitting on the curb with everything he owns in a bag, an old woman alone in a hospital corridor. For some people, for a second, something in the chest actually moves: a small, physical lurch. Then the thumb keeps scrolling, and the feeling fades. That first second is what today's word is about. The old manual says it's where the word itself comes from.
screen: `A PHOTO STOPS YOU.` → `SOMETHING IN THE CHEST MOVES.` → `THEN THE THUMB SCROLLS ON.`

segments.voice: Karuna is compassion, the second of the four rooms. The Visuddhimagga gives it a playful etymology, the way old commentators liked to. When others suffer, it says, compassion makes the hearts of good people tremble, and that trembling is karuna. Another explanation: it's called karuna because it fights, or scatters, others' pain. Modern scholars might trace the word differently, but the manual's point is about experience: compassion starts in the body, as that small lurch in the chest. Its mark, the map says, is the wish to remove suffering. Its job is not being able to bear another's pain. It shows up as harmlessness, and it grows from seeing people who are overwhelmed. A story in the monastic rules shows what that looks like. The Buddha and his attendant Ananda were walking through the monks' lodgings and found a monk lying sick with dysentery, in his own mess, with no one caring for him. The other monks had left him, the story says, because he was no use to them. The Buddha didn't give a talk. He sent Ananda for water, and together they washed the man and laid him on a bed. Then he gathered the monks and said, in effect: you have no mother or father here to care for you; if you don't care for each other, who will? And he added a line: whoever would care for me should care for the sick. So karuna isn't only a feeling. The trembling heart is where it starts. The water and the washing are where it goes.
screen: `THE HEART THAT TREMBLES.` · `THE WISH TO REMOVE SUFFERING.` · `THE SICK MONK, LEFT ALONE.` · `WHOEVER WOULD CARE FOR ME.` · then, large: `THE HEART TREMBLES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you know who is having a hard time, and picture them going through an ordinary day with it. Let the heart tremble a little, without pushing the feeling away or drowning in it. If words help, offer one: may you be free from this pain.
Karuna. Compassion: the heart that trembles at another's pain, and the wish to take that pain away.
Your line: the heart trembles. First the trembling, then the water. That's day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Pity is not compassion
236.hook: compassion's near enemy is pity or sorrow; its far enemy is cruelty (Visuddhimagga 9)
236.tomorrow: Compassion for the one who harms
236.howItsDone: Meditation teachers use the Visuddhimagga's near and far enemies to help students tell compassion from sorrow and pity; some Buddhist chaplains and caregivers describe their work as being present beside someone rather than rescuing from above.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karuna, the heart that trembles, and the Buddha washing a sick monk. Your line: the heart trembles. Today, its two enemies.

Have you ever been on the receiving end of the head tilt? You share something hard, and the other person tilts their head, lowers their voice, and says, oh, you poor thing. They mean well. But the one on the receiving end can feel smaller: they came as an equal and somehow left as a charity case. Compare the friend who just sits down next to you and says, that's awful, I'm here. Both are responses to pain. Only one of them feels like company.
screen: `THE HEAD TILT.` → `OH, YOU POOR THING.` → `THE FRIEND WHO SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Like every room, compassion has two enemies. The Visuddhimagga names the far enemy first: cruelty, the wish to hurt, the plain opposite of the trembling heart. That one's easy to spot. The near enemy is trickier. The manual's word for it is grief, a sorrow tied to one's own worldly life, domanassa. It's near because both compassion and grief see someone's misfortune. But grief turns the pain toward yourself: how awful, how sad this makes me. Compassion keeps its eyes on the other person, and on what would help. So the manual says compassion succeeds when it makes cruelty fade, and fails when it just produces sorrow. Some modern teachers add a close cousin: pity. Pity also sees misfortune, but it looks down from a safe height. It says, I'm glad that's not me. It keeps a little distance, a little ranking, between the one who suffers and the one who feels sorry. Compassion closes that distance. It knows the same things can happen to anyone: sickness, loss, old age, death. Remember the sick monk. The Buddha didn't stand in the doorway looking sad. He had water fetched, and with Ananda washed the man with his own hands and lifted him onto a bed. Beside him, not above. There's a simple test. After you meet someone's pain, do you feel smaller and more burdened, or more connected and more ready to help? The first is sorrow. The second is the room called karuna.
screen: `FAR ENEMY: CRUELTY.` · `NEAR ENEMY: GRIEF, DOMANASSA.` · `PITY LOOKS DOWN FROM A SAFE HEIGHT.` · `WATER, AND HIS OWN HANDS.` · then, large: `BESIDE, NOT ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring back the person you thought of yesterday, and notice where you stand in the picture: looking down at them, a little sorry and a little relieved, or sinking into your own sadness? Gently change the picture: sit down beside them, shoulder to shoulder, on the same ground. From there, offer the wish: may you be free from this pain.
Domanassa. Grief, a sorrow tied to our own worldly life: compassion's near enemy, sorrow that turns inward, and pity that looks down; compassion sits beside.
Your line: beside, not above. Same ground, same kind of life, shoulder to shoulder. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 236 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: COMPASSION FOR THE ONE WHO HARMS.`

237.title: Compassion for the one who harms
237.hook: the manuals: feel compassion even for a wrongdoer, who is heading toward suffering
237.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers encourage extending compassion even to people who do harm, starting with small cases, while being clear that this doesn't excuse harm or require staying near danger; the Angulimala story is widely told, and a verse linked to him is chanted for safe childbirth in Theravada communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: domanassa, the sorrow that turns inward, and pity that looks down. Your line: beside, not above. Today, the hardest case.

Compassion for the sick is easy to understand. For the grieving, the lost, the frightened: of course. But what about the person who cheated, lied, hurt someone you love? When they finally get what's coming, the feeling can be closer to satisfaction. The old Buddhist manual goes somewhere that can feel almost backward at first. The one doing harm, it says, is someone to feel compassion for too. Not because harm doesn't matter. Because of where it leads.
screen: `COMPASSION FOR THE SICK: EASY.` → `FOR THE ONE WHO CHEATED?` → `THE MANUAL GOES FURTHER.`

segments.voice: The Visuddhimagga gives a picture. A thief has been caught, and is being led through the streets to his execution. People who see him feel a pang, the manual says: that poor man is walking to his death. Now look at anyone who does harm the same way. Even if they're laughing now, rich and comfortable, they are walking toward suffering, because in Buddhist teaching, harmful actions ripen into pain for the one who does them. So this compassion isn't approval. It's seeing where the road goes. A story in the suttas shows what this looks like in person. In the Buddha's time, a man called Angulimala was terrorizing a region of Kosala, killing people and, the story says, wearing a garland of their fingers. People along the road warned the Buddha not to go on. He walked it anyway. Angulimala chased him, running as hard as he could, and couldn't catch up with the Buddha, who was only walking. He shouted, stop! And the Buddha said: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. Those words broke something open. Angulimala threw away his weapons and became a monk. The story doesn't say his actions vanished; people still threw stones at him on his alms rounds, and the Buddha told him to bear it. Compassion doesn't cancel consequences, and it doesn't mean staying near someone dangerous. It means that, from a safe distance, you can still see a person walking toward pain, and wish them a different road.
screen: `THE THIEF LED TO EXECUTION.` · `HARM RIPENS INTO PAIN.` · `ANGULIMALA: I HAVE STOPPED.` · `COMPASSION DOESN'T CANCEL CONSEQUENCES.` · then, large: `THEY ARE HEADING FOR PAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has done a small harm, not the worst person you know, and not someone who hurt you deeply; the manuals say to start small. See the road they're on, where behavior like that usually leads, loneliness, fear, more trouble, and let the heart tremble a little for where they're heading. If you can, offer one breath of the wish, may you find a different road, and then let them go.
Angulimala. The killer turned monk whom the Buddha didn't flee, telling him simply: I have stopped, you stop too.
Your line: they are heading for pain. Not approval: a wish for a different road. Two hundred thirty-seven days, and counting.

238.title: Mudita
238.hook: sympathetic joy: gladness at someone else's good fortune
238.howItsDone: Buddhists practice mudita by rejoicing in others' happiness and good deeds; in many Theravada communities people say 'sadhu, sadhu, sadhu' to rejoice in someone else's merit, and teachers offer mudita as a meditation starting with a dear friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angulimala, the killer who heard, I have stopped; you stop too. Your line: they are heading for pain. Today, the end of the week, and the third room.

A friend texts: I got the job. Or: we're engaged. Or: the scan was clear. For a split second, before you type the exclamation points, something happens inside. Sometimes it's pure gladness. Sometimes there's a small, uninvited flicker: why not me? Its darker cousin, pleasure at someone else's trouble, is familiar enough that English borrowed a German word for it. For the good opposite, joy at someone else's good fortune, English has no everyday word at all. Pali does.
screen: `I GOT THE JOB.` → `A SMALL FLICKER: WHY NOT ME?` → `ENGLISH HAS NO WORD.`

segments.voice: Mudita comes from a root meaning to be glad, to rejoice. It's usually translated sympathetic joy, or appreciative joy: gladness at another's happiness and success. It's the third of the four rooms. The Visuddhimagga's map says mudita's mark is gladness, and its job is to be free of envy. It shows up as the end of discontent, the sour feeling that someone else's good news somehow takes something away from you. Its ground is seeing other people's success. Here's what makes mudita unusual. Kindness wishes that people be happy. Compassion wishes that they be free from pain. Mudita meets people who already are happy, and simply agrees. It's joy you didn't have to earn, available every time anyone, anywhere, has a good day. Some teachers call it the most overlooked of the four rooms, because people assume they'd feel it naturally, and then discover the little flicker of why not me. The manual's advice is practical. Start with someone you're already close to, a dear friend whose good news makes you easily glad. Then widen the circle: a neutral person, then someone difficult. And practice when you see someone happy, or hear good news about them, so the gladness has something real to rest on. This week walked through two and a half rooms: the four divine abodes; metta and its near enemy, clinging; its far enemy, ill will; karuna, the trembling heart; pity, which looks down, and compassion, which sits beside; compassion even for the one who harms. Now mudita.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a dear friend who's had good news lately, or who's simply happy right now, and picture their face when things are going well. Let yourself be glad with them, notice how that gladness feels in your own body, and if words help, offer one: may your happiness continue. If you like, widen it to someone you barely know, enjoying a good day.
Mudita. Sympathetic joy: gladness at someone else's good fortune, joy you didn't have to earn.
Your line: their joy is joy. And it can be yours too. That's the week.
